card.hook: Everyone queues up for turtles in the main bay, but the best turquoise might be next door, with a lot fewer elbows. Half Moon Bay is the quiet one, and the water looks like a swimming-pool ad.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject: Half Moon Bay, the quieter bay next to the main Akumal Bay, which you reach on foot from the shore. Face the water so the curve of the shoreline sits in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the whole sweep of the bay, then try 1x for a calmer, more natural look. Zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) is handy for a far-off swimmer or a line of palms.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom line, and tap the brightest patch of water, then slide it a little darker so the sand doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Check conditions on the day, because seaweed can sometimes collect along the shore. A clear, clean stretch of water makes the best shot.
card.selfie_here: Try the path near the old cannons at the northern point of Akumal Bay. Use the front camera at 0.5x, face out over the water, and let the bay fill the frame behind you. If the cannons feel too busy, a palm leaning over the sea just south of the bay is a nice backup, with the open water behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on the public path in front of the Centro Ecológico Akumal, at the corner of the bay, to take your picture with the bay and cannon area in view.
card.rules_and_safety: Beach access is regulated: guests of beachfront hotels get free access, while others may need to pay through a private establishment (reported at 140 pesos). Rules can change, so check local guidance first. The cannon area is disputed, as some say it's private property and a guard may stop you, so be polite and move on if asked. Turtle nests are protected, so keep your distance from turtles and wildlife and shoot from the shore.
card.challenge: Get a shot where the horizon is perfectly level and the water takes up most of the frame, with just one strip of sand at the bottom.
card.good_to_know: Akumal began in 1958 as a community for scuba divers, on the site of a former coconut plantation. Green sea turtles come into the bay to feed on sea grass. Akumal Bay was declared a marine refuge in 2016 to protect them.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject: Half Moon Bay, the quieter bay next to the main Akumal Bay, which you reach on foot from the shore. Face the water so the curve of the shoreline sits in front of you.

selfie_research.notes: Akumal is a bay and beach town rather than a single landmark, so the spots are around the bay. The cannon area is disputed: one forum says they are on private property, while another says the walkway beside them is public; a guard may stop you. The forum says the bay itself requires crossing private land. The palm spot is a blogger's photo, so its view of the bay is inferred, not stated. card.hook: Most people come to Xel-Há to swim, but the best photo here is the one you take while you're still dry. Stop halfway across the floating bridge and look at all that turquoise.
card.stand_here: Stand on the floating bridge that crosses the snorkelling lagoon. Face out over the water, so the turquoise stretches away from the walkway with jungle trees along both edges.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit in the whole lagoon and the trees around it. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural look. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) picks out a far stretch of shoreline or people snorkelling.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom line with plenty of water in front, then tap the water and nudge it a little darker so the turquoise keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Check the park's official site for opening times and how busy it's likely to be. Fewer people in the shot makes for a cleaner photo.
card.selfie_here: Cross the floating bridge to the oversized chair and sit in it for a playful photo with the park and lagoon behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit lower so more of the scene fits over your shoulder. You can also pose beside the Xel-Há sign inside the park, which puts the name in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Xel-Há is a paid park, so you need park admission to reach the floating bridge. Hold your phone firmly with both hands over the water, and think about a wrist strap. If you jump from the cliff, only do it at the spot where a lifeguard is watching.
card.challenge: Take one shot where the bridge rail leads your eye right into the lagoon, then see if you can get it with nobody walking through.
card.good_to_know: The name comes from Yucatec Maya words for "spring" and "water". Long before it was a park, it was a Maya settlement, occupied by the 1st century, and it served as a port for the Maya city of Coba, alongside Tancah and Tulum. In 1527 the Spanish conquistador Francisco de Montejo landed here and tried to found a settlement, but the camp was abandoned within about eighteen months.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the floating bridge that crosses the snorkelling lagoon. Face out over the water, so the turquoise stretches away from the walkway with jungle trees along both edges. The phone icon may sit a little off the bridge, so trust the bridge itself.

card.hook: Picture a stone temple perched on a 12-metre cliff with the turquoise Caribbean right behind it. That's Tulum, and one frame gets you the history and the sea together.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the east-facing base of the pyramid, El Castillo, and face out over the water. The sea is straight ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the cliff and the sea both fit. If the paths are busy and you can't step back, try zoom 0.5x. Zoom 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) gets you a tighter shot of the temple's top and doorways.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the temple, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sea stays blue instead of washing out.
card.best_time: Go at 8-9 AM, when the morning light hits the main face of the temple. You'll also have fewer tour groups to dodge.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and tilt your phone so the landmark sits over your shoulder. Try 0.5x if your phone offers it, so more of the scene squeezes in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a protected archaeological site, so there are likely entry rules. Check the official INAH site for entry fees, photo and drone rules, and beach access before you go. Beach access depends on conditions and tides.
card.challenge: Switch on gridlines and put the horizon on a third line, perfectly level, with a little sky above the ruins. Bonus points if nobody's head sneaks into the frame.
card.good_to_know: Tulum was a walled Maya port city, at its greatest between the 13th and 15th centuries and abandoned by the end of the 16th. The landward wall averaged 3-5 metres high and about 8 metres thick. In 1843 the explorers Stephens and Catherwood arrived by sea and were struck by a tall building, most likely El Castillo.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the east-facing base of the pyramid, El Castillo, and face out over the water. The sea is straight ahead of you.

card.hook: Turquoise water, cool rock and soft cave light all in one frame, and about a hundred other people trying to get the same shot. Gran Cenote is gorgeous, so here's how to find your own quiet corner.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon on the map, which sits right at Gran Cenote itself. For a calmer picture, walk to the smaller area to the right of the cenote stairs and face the pool with the cave behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the pool and the cave together, especially from the wooden platform. Use 1x for a natural view of the water and cave opening, then 2x for close details like light on the water or the shapes in the rock.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the water, then slide it a little darker so the glowing turquoise keeps its colour (and wipe your phone's camera glass first, because the air is damp).
card.best_time: We can't give you a perfect hour, so go when it's quieter. The cave light changes through the day, so take a look as you arrive and see what you've got.
card.selfie_here: Walk out on the wooden bridge and rail over the clear blue water in the second open-air cavern, a popular photo spot. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the bridge and water behind you. The second sinkhole, through the small tunnel, is also good for pictures and tends to be less busy.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to take your photo on the famous cenote staircase, where a line often forms, so arrive early to keep other people out of the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Guides say phone photos are allowed and that you must shower before getting in, but rules can change, so check on the day. Wear water shoes, because the rocks can be a little sharp.
card.challenge: Take two shots: one wide of the whole scene, then one close-up of just the water and rock, and see which one you like more.
card.good_to_know: Gran Cenote is a natural swimming spot in the Tulum area, with clear turquoise water in a cave setting. The main area is the busiest part, so the quieter corners are the best place to take your time. It's a paid-entry site, so check the current rules and entry details on the day.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the phone icon on the map, which sits right at Gran Cenote itself. For a calmer picture, walk to the smaller area to the right of the cenote stairs and face the pool with the cave behind it.

card.hook: Picture two huge blue eyes staring up out of the jungle floor. That's Dos Ojos, which means 'Two Eyes', and yes, the name fits. Your phone is going to love the glowing water against the dark rock.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, then pick your eye. For the classic view, face the bright cavern entrance of the first (east) eye. For the moodier one, walk through the gallery to the second (west) eye and face the pool.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the cavern opening, the water and the rock around it. Switch to 1x for a natural view of the water and the boardwalk. If your phone has 2x or 5x, use it for close shots of single stalactites or ripples.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the water in the lower third and let the stalactites fill the top, then tap the bright water and drag the slider a little darker so the blues stay rich.
card.best_time: Weekends can get crowded, so a weekday may mean fewer people in the water. Check the official site before you go for current hours and conditions.
card.selfie_here: Try the wooden boardwalk at the top of the stairs down into the first (east) eye, at the entrance to the largest cave. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the cavern over your shoulder. One travel blog recommends this spot, so check how it looks when you get there.
card.rules_and_safety: The wet wood around the swim areas can be slippery, so walk carefully there. Dos Ojos is a managed park that may be ticketed and may have its own photo rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one photo of each eye and see which one wins: bright and classic, or dark and dramatic.
card.good_to_know: The two cenotes open into one large shared cavern. The water stays at about 25 °C all year and is only around 10 metres deep near the openings, which is why the turquoise is so easy to see. The cave system beneath has been explored since 1987 and appeared in the BBC series Planet Earth.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, then pick your eye. For the classic view, face the bright cavern entrance of the first (east) eye. For the moodier one, walk through the gallery to the second (west) eye and face the pool.

card.hook: Here's a neat trick for a Tulum photo that needs no caption: stand where a small, detailed temple sits in front of the big, famous one. The Temple of the Frescoes does that job, with El Castillo looming behind it.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon on the map, which marks the Temple of the Frescoes itself, then step back to the southeast side. Face the front of the temple and keep El Castillo beside it in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the temple and El Castillo both fit and look natural. Use 0.5x only if people or ropes force you to stand close. Then try 2x, if your phone has it, for the stucco figures and corner masks.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the temple, then slide the picture a little darker if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Go early, soon after opening, for better light and fewer people walking through your frame. If you're there later, one guide suggests the west-facing side for warmer late-day light.
card.selfie_here: Try the path in front of the temple's main facade, near the grass hut by the entrance, where the stelae and the Descending God niches make a recognisable backdrop. Use the front camera (0.5x if yours has it), hold it a bit low and let the temple sit over your shoulder. Nobody has written up a pose here, so treat it as a good guess and see what works on the day.
card.rules_and_safety: You need to enter the Tulum archaeological zone, so check the official site for current rules before you go. The murals inside are closed to visitors, so this is an outside-only photo, and flash is discouraged near the frescoes, so switch it off. Bring water and sun protection, because the sun can be strong and there's limited shade around the ruins.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with both buildings, then a close-up of a corner mask, and see if you can make the pair look like a before-and-after.
card.good_to_know: The Temple of the Frescoes sits right in front of El Castillo inside the Tulum archaeological zone. Its outer walls carry stucco figures and corner masks. The painted murals inside are closed to protect them, which is why you photograph it from outside.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon on the map, which marks the Temple of the Frescoes itself, then step back to the southeast side. Face the front of the temple and keep El Castillo beside it in the frame.
